title: Animal Disease and Australian Biosecurity
subtitle: Why the dead animals are the smaller bill
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: assess the causes and effects of diseases on agricultural production, including but not limited to: animal diseases
investigate procedures that can be employed to prevent the spread of disease, including but not limited to: quarantine
Explain procedures employed in Australia to limit transmission of infectious diseases in animals and plants
lessonIntent: Students can name major livestock diseases by pathogen type, separate direct from indirect effects, and explain the pre-border, border and post-border procedures Australia uses to limit transmission of disease in animals and plants.
examSkill: Explain how named Australian biosecurity procedures limit disease transmission, and assess the direct and indirect effects of an animal disease outbreak.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, animal disease and Australian biosecurity. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: An 8 billion pound disease
scenes.body: In 2001 foot-and-mouth disease hit UK livestock. Millions of animals were culled, and the total cost dwarfed their value.
scenes.callout: Why is biosecurity so relentless at the border?
scenes.caption: The 2001 UK foot-and-mouth outbreak cost about 8 billion pounds, far more than the culled animals.

voiceover.text: In two thousand and one, foot and mouth disease tore through livestock across the United Kingdom. Over six million animals were culled, the countryside was closed to visitors, and export markets were shut. The final bill came to around eight billion pounds, far more than the animals themselves were worth. Australia has been free of foot and mouth since eighteen seventy two, and government estimates put the cost of a large outbreak here in the tens of billions of dollars. So how does Australia keep diseases like this out, and stop them spreading if they do arrive? That's the biosecurity system we're unpacking today.

scenes.heading: Direct versus indirect effects
scenes.body: Animal disease hurts production two ways, and for an exporter like Australia, the indirect side dominates.

bullets.text: Direct: animal death, reduced productivity, and treatment or culling costs.
Indirect: export bans, movement restrictions, and lost consumer confidence.
For Australia, lost export markets usually exceed the cost of the animals.

scenes.secondary: In the 2001 UK outbreak, lost tourism and trade pushed the total cost far beyond the value of the animals culled.
scenes.callout: Split every cost: direct, then indirect.
scenes.caption: Direct costs are animals and treatment; indirect costs are trade bans and lost markets.

voiceover.text: Here's the framework for assessing the effects, and it's about splitting the cost in two. The direct effects are the obvious ones, animals dying, sick animals producing less milk, meat or wool, and the costs of treatment and culling. The indirect effects are usually bigger, especially for an exporter. Importing countries shut their doors the moment a notifiable disease is detected, movement restrictions stop animals being sold or transported, and consumer confidence drops even for unaffected produce. For Australia, which exports a large share of its beef and lamb, lost market access almost always outweighs the direct cost of the animals. That's exactly why so much effort goes into prevention.

scenes.heading: The terms you need

bullets.text: Biosecurity: measures that stop pests and diseases entering, establishing and spreading.
Notifiable disease: one that must be reported to authorities by law.
Quarantine: isolating animals, plants or goods that may carry disease.
Traceability: tracking where animals have been, so an outbreak can be traced fast.

scenes.callout: Keep it out, find it fast, stop it spreading.
scenes.caption: Biosecurity, notifiable disease, quarantine, traceability.

voiceover.text: Four terms underpin this lesson. Biosecurity is the whole set of measures that stop pests and diseases entering a country, establishing, and spreading. A notifiable disease is one that, by law, must be reported to authorities, and foot and mouth is the prime example. Quarantine means isolating animals, plants or goods that might carry disease until they're shown to be safe. And traceability is the ability to track where animals have been and which animals they've mixed with, so that an outbreak can be traced and contained quickly. Put simply, biosecurity is about keeping disease out, finding it fast, and stopping it spreading.

scenes.heading: Major livestock diseases
scenes.body: The HSC expects you to name livestock diseases with their pathogen type and main impact.

bullets.text: Foot-and-mouth: a virus in cloven-hoofed animals, highly contagious.
Bovine tuberculosis: a bacterium in cattle, eradicated here by test and cull.
Avian influenza: a virus in birds; highly pathogenic strains kill most of a flock.

scenes.secondary: Hydatid disease is caused by a tapeworm cycling between dogs and sheep. The pathogen type shapes whether you vaccinate, test and cull, or break the life cycle.
scenes.callout: Name it, then state its type and impact.
scenes.caption: Foot-and-mouth, bovine TB, avian influenza and hydatid disease span different pathogen types.

voiceover.text: You'll need to name livestock diseases with their pathogen type, so let's run the key ones. Foot and mouth disease is caused by a virus that affects cloven hoofed animals like cattle, pigs and sheep, and it's extremely contagious, spreading by contact, in the air, and on vehicles, clothing and animal products. Bovine tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium, and was eradicated from Australian cattle through test and cull programs. Avian influenza is a virus of birds, and highly pathogenic strains can kill almost an entire poultry flock. And hydatid disease is caused by a tapeworm, a macroorganism, forming cysts in the organs of sheep and cattle. Notice that the pathogen type shapes the response, whether you vaccinate, test and cull, or break a life cycle.

scenes.heading: Australia's biosecurity layers
scenes.body: Australia limits transmission in animals and plants at three layers: before the border, at the border, and after it.

bullets.text: Pre-border: import risk assessments, permits and overseas checks.
Border: inspection, detector dogs, X-ray screening and quarantine of imports.
Post-border: surveillance, reporting, traceability, movement controls and zoning.

scenes.secondary: Plants get the same treatment: fruit fly and other pest zones restrict moving produce between regions, and exotic plant pests must be reported.
scenes.callout: Keep it out, find it fast, stop it spreading.
scenes.caption: Pre-border, border and post-border biosecurity limit transmission in animals and plants.

voiceover.text: So what does Australia actually do? Think of biosecurity as three layers. Before the border, imports are risk assessed, so some products need permits or treatment overseas, and some are banned outright. At the border, travellers and cargo are inspected, using declarations, detector dogs and X ray screening, and risky animals, plants and goods are quarantined, treated or destroyed. After the border, the focus is surveillance and control. Vets and farmers must report notifiable diseases, northern Australia is monitored closely because it's nearest to our neighbours, and the National Livestock Identification System tags cattle, sheep and goats so their movements can be traced. Plants get the same logic, with pest free zones that restrict moving fruit between regions to stop fruit fly. And on farms, biosecurity plans mean isolating new stock, controlling visitors and cleaning vehicles.

Detector dogs find meat in luggage
Inspection of fruit and plant material

scenes.heading: Respond to an FMD detection
scenes.question: Foot-and-mouth disease is confirmed in Australian cattle. Explain the procedures that would limit its transmission, and assess the likely economic effects.
scenes.coachNote: Name each procedure and link it to how it breaks transmission, then split effects into direct and indirect.
steps: Report and stop: the case is notified, and a national livestock standstill halts all susceptible animal movements.
Contain: quarantine zones around infected farms; NLIS traces animals that moved on or off those farms.
Eliminate: infected and exposed animals are culled and farms decontaminated; vaccination may be used to limit spread.
Effects: direct costs are culling and lost production; indirect costs are export bans and lost disease-free status.
Conclusion: fast tracing and movement controls limit spread, but indirect trade losses would still dominate the cost.
scenes.caption: Notify, standstill, quarantine zones, trace, cull and decontaminate; trade losses still dominate.

voiceover.text: Let's apply this to a foot and mouth detection in Australian cattle. First, the case is reported, because it's notifiable, and a national livestock standstill stops all susceptible animals moving, which cuts off the main route for spread. Next, containment. Quarantine zones are set up around infected farms, and the livestock identification system traces every animal that moved on or off those farms recently, so exposed herds can be found fast. Then elimination. Infected and exposed animals are culled, farms are decontaminated, and vaccination may be used to slow spread. Now the effects. The direct costs are the culled animals and lost production. The indirect costs are bigger, because export markets close and our disease free status disappears overnight. So the conclusion is that fast tracing and movement controls limit transmission, but the trade losses would still dominate the bill.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking the main cost of animal disease is the animals themselves. For an exporter, lost markets are almost always larger.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: thinking Australia is protected simply by being an island. Diseases arrive in luggage, cargo, animals and on the wind, so active biosecurity does the real work.
scenes.callout: Lost markets beat lost animals; geography alone won't save you.
scenes.caption: Lost markets usually exceed animal losses; active biosecurity, not geography, protects Australia.

voiceover.text: Two traps to finish. Trap one, assuming the main damage from an animal disease is the animals that die or get culled. For an export dependent country like Australia, the bigger cost is almost always lost markets, and a single foot and mouth detection would trigger export bans worth far more than the animals. Trap two, assuming Australia is safe simply because it's an island. Geography helps, but diseases arrive in contaminated meat in a traveller's luggage, in cargo, in imported animals and plant material, and some pests can even be blown in on the wind from neighbouring countries. So the real protection comes from active biosecurity, meaning border screening, surveillance and fast response.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Foot-and-mouth disease is a livestock disease, yet Australian airports screen passengers' luggage for pork and beef products. Explain how this procedure limits transmission.
answerSteps: The FMD virus can survive in raw, chilled, frozen and cured meat products.
Contaminated meat brought in by a traveller could be fed to pigs, infecting them.
Infected pigs release large amounts of virus, spreading it to cattle and sheep.
Screening with declarations, detector dogs and X-rays removes this entry route at the border; banning swill feeding blocks the next step.
Answer: the procedure stops the virus entering in food, breaking transmission before it reaches livestock ✓
scenes.caption: Luggage screening stops FMD entering in meat products before it can reach livestock.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Foot and mouth is a livestock disease, yet airports screen passengers' luggage for pork and beef products. Explain how this procedure limits transmission. Pause and reason it through. Okay, here's the logic. The foot and mouth virus can survive in raw, frozen and cured meat. If contaminated meat slipped through and was fed to pigs, they'd be infected, and infected pigs pump out huge amounts of virus that can spread to cattle and sheep. So screening luggage, using declarations, detector dogs and X rays, removes that entry route at the border, and Australia's ban on feeding food scraps to pigs blocks the next step. The answer is that the procedure stops the virus entering in food, breaking the chain before it ever reaches livestock.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Animal disease has direct effects, animals and treatment, and indirect effects, trade and markets.
For an exporter like Australia, indirect effects usually dominate.
Know key diseases by type: FMD and avian flu are viral, bovine TB bacterial, hydatid a tapeworm.
Biosecurity works in layers: pre-border, border and post-border, for animals and plants.
Reporting, standstills, quarantine zones and NLIS tracing limit spread once a disease arrives.
scenes.finalPrompt: Explaining a biosecurity procedure? Name it, then say exactly which transmission route it breaks.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: direct vs indirect, exporter impact, diseases by type, biosecurity layers, outbreak response.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. First, animal disease has direct effects, the animals and their treatment, and indirect effects, the trade bans and lost markets. Second, for an export dependent nation like Australia, the indirect effects usually dominate. Third, know the key diseases by pathogen type, foot and mouth and avian influenza are viral, bovine TB is bacterial, and hydatid disease is caused by a tapeworm. Fourth, Australian biosecurity works in layers, before the border, at the border and after it, for animals and plants alike. And fifth, once a disease arrives, reporting, movement standstills, quarantine zones and livestock tracing limit its spread. Whenever you explain a procedure, name it, then say exactly which transmission route it breaks. See you next lesson.
